one_liner: Tiny embeddable C99 bytecode VM with Ruby-flavoured Python syntax; roughly CPython speed, well behind Lua 5.3.
what_it_does: Pocketlang is a dynamically typed, object-oriented scripting language (classes, closures, fibers, modules, tail calls) whose compiler, bytecode VM and runtime build into one standalone executable or a static library with no external dependencies. The host embeds it through a small C API (pkNewConfiguration, pkNewVM, pkRunString/pkRunFile, slot-based native functions, pluggable realloc, stdout and script-loader callbacks). It is a different language, not a drop-in for Python, Lua or any existing runtime.
how_it_is_fast: Values are NaN-boxed 64-bit words (VAR_NAN_TAGGING on by default in internal.h), so numbers, booleans and null need no heap allocation. The compiler emits a stack-based bytecode with single-byte operands, and locals and module globals are read and written by array index (PUSH_GLOBAL/STORE_GLOBAL index into module->globals), not by name lookup. Return-position calls compile to TAIL_CALL so tail recursion reuses the frame. Dispatch is a plain switch inside a goto loop (no computed goto), arithmetic goes through out-of-line varAdd/varModulo helpers, and every number is a double (the integer tag is defined but unused), so there is no special integer fast path.
when_to_use: Embedding a small scripting layer in a C or C++ host where a single dependency-free C99 source tree (cli/, src/core/, src/libs/) is the main requirement and CPython-class speed is acceptable.
Configuration, glue or game-logic scripts where users expect Python/Ruby-like syntax rather than Lua's.
Tail-recursive code: TAIL_CALL reuses the caller's frame, so deep tail recursion does not grow the stack.
Browser demos or sandboxes via the existing Emscripten/WebAssembly build.
Teaching or studying a compact Crafting-Interpreters-style VM (about 12k lines in src/core) that you are willing to own and patch.
when_not_to_use: When you need more speed than CPython: in the only readable numbers (issue #140) it was slower than Python on list and primes, tied on fib, and Lua 5.3.4 was 3.2x to 6.8x faster on all five benchmarks.
Integer-heavy code: all numbers are doubles, % is fmod, and integers are exact only up to 2^53.

Running untrusted scripts: open issue #302 (2026-02-11) reports a heap-buffer-overflow in pkByteBufferAddString on an unterminated string, a NULL function-pointer call in parsePrecedence and a crash in varContains, with no maintainer reply.
Projects that need a maintained runtime: feature work stopped in June 2022, the 'Abandoned?' issue #298 (2024) has no reply, 30 issues and 28 PRs are open, and the language is still version 0.1.0.
Large scripts: the compiler caps a scope at 256 variables, 256 upvalues and 256 break statements, and global indices are single bytes.

integration.form: source-drop (Makefile also builds a static lib, libpocketlang.a, and a CLI)
integration.dependencies: none (libm and libdl on *nix; cJSON and cwalk are vendored in src/libs/thirdparty)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (GCC, Clang, MinGW, MSVC; Emscripten for WebAssembly)
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux, macOS (the benchmark runner accepts only these three), WebAssembly; any 64-bit target where NaN-boxed pointers fit in 48 bits
integration.thread_safety: not documented; state lives in a per-instance PKVM with its own configuration, so separate VMs per thread look feasible but this is untested here

gotchas: Harness asymmetry: factors.py and loop.py run their hot loops at module scope (CPython dict-based global name lookups), while the .pk scripts get index-addressed globals and the .lua scripts use locals; the two benchmarks pocketlang wins against Python in issue #140 (factors 1.32x, loop 1.79x) are exactly these two, and on the three function-bodied benchmarks (fib, list, primes) it ties or loses. The wins likely measure Python's module-scope penalty more than the VM.

scripts/run_benchmarks.py runs each interpreter once with no repetition or warm-up and trusts each script's self-printed 'elapsed:' line; pocketlang times with C clock() (CPU time on POSIX, wall time under MSVC on Windows, where the README chart was made) while Python uses process_time and Ruby uses Time.now, so the clocks differ by platform. The Lua scripts are not line-for-line ports (loop.lua fills by index instead of appending).

Build mode matters and is easy to get wrong: plain 'make' builds the Debug target (-Og with DEBUG assertions) and the README's one-line gcc command passes no -O flag; the benchmark runner expects build/Release/bin/pocket from 'make release' (-g -O3). Issue #140 does not say which build it used.
Range loops ('for i in 2..n') allocate a Range object per loop entry and iterate with doubles; the WebAssembly build disables input, file handling and relative import.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Wren or pocketpy only when you specifically want its Ruby-flavoured Python syntax in a few thousand lines of C99 and accept unmaintained code; Wren has an independent re-run showing it ahead of Lua 5.4.4 and CPython 3.11.3, and pocketpy offers real Python syntax with a measured edge over CPython 3.8.10. For speed alone, LuaJIT or stock Lua beat it by a wide margin.
verified_claims_summary: A third-party run in issue #140 (2021-06-25, the day after the benchmark scripts were last changed; no hardware, Python version or pocketlang build mode given) timed the repo's five scripts: pocketlang beat CPython on factors (4.00 s vs 5.27 s) and loop (1.23 s vs 2.20 s), tied on fib (3.04 vs 3.03) and lost on list (2.88 vs 2.59) and primes (3.74 vs 2.91), while Lua 5.3.4 took 0.39 to 0.95 s on every test. The README's own chart (pre-alpha pocketlang vs Wren 0.3.0, Python 3.7.4, Ruby 2.7.2 on an i7-6700HQ under Windows 10) is an image that could not be read here (user-images.githubusercontent.com blocked).
status_note: Effectively unmaintained since June 2022 (one 2026-01-03 commit adds native API docs and build changes, and a 2026 memory-safety report is unanswered), but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small enough to vendor if you are prepared to fix crashes yourself.
